description: Hello,we are a team of four. A team consisting of madness and obviously a lot of curiosity.
summary: Earthpulse is an interactive website that turns twenty years of NASA Earth science data into a guide for spotting real significant trends. We used NASA’s Giovanni portal to collect monthly records from January 2006 to January 2026 for 23 of Earth’s most extreme places, such as Furnace Creek, Mawsynram, Mount Everest and the Pantanal. The records cover nine variables, from air temperature and rainfall to soil wetness, wind and pressure. Our Python code cleans missing values, removes the seasonal cycle, fits a linear trend and tests whether it is statistically significant using the T-test. The website lets anyone walk through this method step by step and filter all 23 results. Users can zoom into any period on the charts, overlay places and download the data. It found significant trends in 9 of the 23 records, and showed that one variable can move in opposite directions in different regions. Earthpulse helps people tell trend from noise.
details:
Project details: Earthpulse

What it does and how it works
Earthpulse is a website that answers one question for 23 extreme places on Earth: is it actually changing? We downloaded 20 years of monthly data (January 2006 to January 2026) from NASA's Giovanni portal. It covers nine variables: air temperature, near-surface air temperature, rainfall rate, root-zone and surface soil wetness, relative humidity, cloud amount, wind speed and surface pressure. Each variable was measured at benchmark places such as Furnace Creek, Mawsynram, the Dead Sea, Mount Everest and the Pantanal.

Every record goes through the same analysis:

  1. Clean: missing values are removed, and gaps of up to two months are filled from the neighboring months.
  2. Remove the seasons: each calendar month's long-term average is subtracted, which leaves the "anomaly".
  3. Fit a trend: a straight line is fitted through the anomalies with linear regression, which gives a rate of change per year.
  4. Test it: the slope is significant if p < 0.05, and we also report a 95% confidence interval and R².

Nine of the 23 records show a significant trend.

The site has two parts:

  • Landing page:
    • an animated walkthrough of the method on any record (raw data → seasons removed → trend line)
    • a filterable grid of all 23 results
    • three good places to start
    • a glossary, and a section on what the results can and cannot tell you
    • pick a topic, variable and place to see the chart, the verdict and a summary in plain English
    • drag a box to zoom into any period, pan, and use keyboard controls
    • overlay other places to compare them
    • download the months you're viewing as a CSV
    • a table showing missing data for each record

Benefits

  • It teaches the difference between a real trend and natural noise. Users rarely see seasonal swings separated from long-term change.
  • It is open: all the raw data and code are on GitHub, and every number on the site is calculated from the data, never typed in by hand.
  • It is easy to reach. It runs in any browser on desktop or phone, with nothing to install, and it works with the keyboard and screen readers.

Intended impact
We want people to read climate data critically: to ask how much, where and how sure are we, not just whether something is "going up". Showing that the same variable can trend in opposite directions in different regions (for example soil wetness in the Pantanal vs. the Sudd) helps people understand that Earth's systems change unevenly.

Teachers can use it as a ready-made classroom tool for statistics and Earth science.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA Giovanni (satellite and model-based Earth observation data), exported as CSV
  • Analysis: Python with pandas (cleaning, removing the seasons) and SciPy (linregress for the trend and significance test)
  • Website: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks. Charts are hand-built SVG, and the animated weather background is drawn on an HTML5 Canvas
  • Hosting and version control: GitHub and Vercel (free static hosting, redeployed automatically on every commit)
  • Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware was needed

How it is creative

  • You see the method happen: instead of just stating "we removed seasonality", the landing page animates the raw data turning into anomalies and then into a trend line, for any record.
  • The page reflects the data: as you scroll the home page, the sky changes through heat, clouds, rain, wind, mist and snow, matching the variables we studied. In the explorer, the sky reflects the variable you choose.
  • Detective-style investigation: in line with the challenge theme: starting cases, comparing places and judging the evidence.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: we used one consistent method for every record, didn't invent or change any values, and flagged inconsistencies instead of guessing (for example, missing months and units inferred from value ranges).
  • Limitations: neighboring months are similar to each other (autocorrelation), so p-values near 0.05 need extra caution. We only test straight-line trends, and 20 years is short in climate terms. These are stated openly on the site.
  • Accessibility: good color contrast, keyboard navigation of the charts, text descriptions of every chart and a layout that works on phones with a simple menu.
  • Usability: plain-language explanations alongside the statistics, so the site works for both beginners and experts.
  • Cost and simplicity: a static site with no server or database. It is fast, free to host and easy for others to reuse.
